items.summary: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.
items.title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents

items.summary: LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming secret reuse scope as the operative vulnerability. We further confirm orbit collapse on two other open-source defenses: the sequence-permutation implementation of Thomas et al. and PermLLM. The KV-Cloak developers invited a detailed report through their private vulnerability reporting channel.
items.title: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches

items.summary: Control-flow integrity (CFI) confines a program to a control-flow graph fixed ahead of time. Procedural agent skills move this control flow into prompt text, and a large language model (LLM) agent decides at runtime whether each step runs in its reasoning, a tool call, or a script. The procedure's control skeleton survives, but its enforceability depends on where each step runs. Many violations, such as overwriting a file before validation, use only operations the skill requires, so permission allowlists admit them. A deviating or prompt-injected model can also evade a monitor by regime migration, for example by claiming that a check passed. We present SkillCFI, which carries CFI over to skill-based agents. Its compiler confines LLM interpretation to compile time and derives the agent's instructions and an executable contract from one skill. By a formal enforceability criterion, it enforces obligations whose evidence crosses the tool boundary and rejects a skill whose mandatory obligation leaves nothing to check. A deterministic runtime enforcer admits a tool request only on trusted evidence and refuses unmediated channels such as inline scripts, so admitted traces follow the contract whatever the model proposes. On eight self-written skills, no compiled contract permits more than its source under 24 source mutations. In 770 agent sessions, SkillCFI blocks before dispatch all 240 such violations, which an allowlist admits, and normal tasks complete nearly as often as without it. Listing the next legal steps in a refusal raises recovery from 21% to 65%. Checking takes about 2% of task time, and a compact command form cuts session slowdown from 1.32 times to 1.08 times. None of 53 public skills is accepted as written. The compiler's diagnostics point to interfaces rather than workflows and guided seven into enforceable contracts.
items.title: Guarding the Kingdom of Skill-Based Agents in the AI Dynasty of Computation: Control-Flow Integrity for Agent Skills

items.summary: As LLM-generated content becomes increasingly widespread, reliable attribution calls for multi-bit watermarks that embed recoverable messages without distorting the output distribution. We introduce PIVOT, a multi-bit watermark with model-free verification based on mirrored rank-interval sampling. At each generation step, PIVOT uses a keyed pseudorandom scalar and a secret permutation of the vocabulary. The message bit determines whether next-token probability intervals are arranged in forward or reverse secret-rank order. Sampling from these mirrored layouts preserves every token probability exactly while inducing an opposite-signed dependence between the scalar and the sampled token's secret rank. This dependence yields a pivotal rank statistic whose null distribution is invariant to the unknown next-token law, enabling model-free calibration and decoding. We formulate joint watermark detection and message recovery as a multiple-hypothesis testing problem, derive a moment-robust minimax-optimal detection score over a relaxed moment class, and establish finite-sample recovery guarantees. Extensive experiments on two representative large language models validate the effectiveness of PIVOT, demonstrating reliable watermark detection and message recovery while preserving the generator's output distribution.
items.title: PIVOT: Distribution-Preserving Multi-BitWatermarking with Minimax-Optimal Scoring

items.summary: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. items.summary: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

items.summary: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at $2^{24}$. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.

items.summary: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

items.summary: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.
items.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security

items.summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .
items.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway

items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.

items.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

items.summary: GitHub natively supports workflow automation through GitHub Actions, now the dominant CI/CD tool on the platform. Yet keeping these workflows secure remains an ongoing burden: maintainers often patch a vulnerability on the default branch but leave the same flaw on the release and maintenance branches that downstream consumers continue to build from. Carrying a known fix onto these divergent branches, called backporting, is rarely done, and this paper presents the first large-scale empirical study quantifying the resulting gap. From a public corpus of GitHub Actions workflow histories, we mine 1,903,191 workflow-modifying commits, scan each before and after with the static scanner zizmor to identify 69,865 security fixes across 24,238 projects, and audit every release branch to check whether each fix was carried over. The gap is pervasive: 224,392 of 474,490 audited release branches remain vulnerable, and deliberate backporting is rare and slow, with only 19,476 of 78,907 already-fixed branches confirmed as plausible backports at a median lag of 243 days. We thus design WorkflowBP, the first technique for automated security-fix backporting of GitHub Actions workflows. WorkflowBP takes a neuro-symbolic approach: it compiles a default-branch fix into a domain-specific representation called the Workflow Semantic Patch (WSP) and applies it to each divergent branch by matching jobs and steps based on their content rather than their position, while an LLM synthesizes the WSP for the most divergent cases the deterministic engine cannot resolve. On 12,000 real unpatched workflow files from our study, WorkflowBP produces a scanner-checked backport for 67.9%. We further submit 176 issues with WorkflowBP-generated backports to real-world projects, 44 of which have been confirmed or fixed by developers.

items.summary: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.
items.title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. Warning: This paper may contain sensitive content.
items.title: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias

items.summary: Is computing a Diffie-Hellman key as hard as computing a discrete logarithm? Maurer showed that it is, given a few bits of advice, provided that short intervals contain enough integers with only small prime factors; that proviso has stood for thirty years. We remove it. For every prime $p$ there is an advice string of $O(\log p)$ bits, depending only on $p$, with which discrete logarithms in every group of order $p$ are computed in polynomial time from a Diffie-Hellman oracle. The reduction is the classical one; what was missing was a proof that short intervals contain polylogarithmically smooth integers. We show that a zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function, which is now known, gives the expected number of $(\log x)^K$-smooth integers in every interval $[x,x+x^θ]$ with $θ>17/30$. With smoothness this small the saddle point of the counting integral lies just to the left of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, and a zero-free strip of any fixed width absorbs the shift once $K$ is large. Genus-2 Jacobians, whose orders fill such intervals, then turn one of these integers into the order of an auxiliary group. The same input removes the smoothness assumption from Maurer and Raub's impossibility of field-homomorphic one-way permutations and from the yes/no-query reduction of Koblitz, Menezes and Shparlinski. It also makes Wolf's characterisation unconditional: discrete logarithm and Diffie-Hellman are generically equivalent exactly when the group order has no large repeated prime factor.
items.title: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Logarithm

items.summary: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.
items.title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation

items.summary: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.
items.title: From Token Changes to Task Failures: Bit Flips in a Shared KV-Cache Block

items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.
items.title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk

items.summary: Hate speech remains a persistent and evolving threat on online platforms. The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outperforming OpenAI's Moderation API on HateBenchSet and MHS. Furthermore, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises its average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%, a gain of 7.7 percentage points, surpassing LlamaGuard-3, Meta's official safety model based on the same Llama-3.1-8B architecture, on three of four benchmarks. These results show that PersonaHate can substantially improve the robustness and cross-dataset generalization of hate speech detectors.
items.title: PersonaHate: A Scalable Persona-Based Data Synthesis Pipeline for Hate Speech Analysis

items.summary: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.
items.title: LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana

items.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.
items.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.
items.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents

items.summary: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. items.summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models

items.summary: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.
items.title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks

Row-count and preview queries execute before confirmUpdate or confirmDelete, allowing malicious arguments to bypass confirmation and maxRows controls and execute stacked DDL or DML, read or destroy data, and potentially run operating-system commands when the SQL login is privileged and xp_cmdshell is enabled. This issue is fixed in core and server version 0.6.0 and reader and writer version 0.5.0.

Prior to 0.11.1, the QUIC/HTTP3 RPC server on the default port 8443 uses tls.RequestClientCert and does not verify that presented certificates chain to the configured cluster certificate authority. The RPC authenticators derive a caller identity from PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName without requiring a non-empty VerifiedChains value, and certificate identities bypass all RBAC checks. A network attacker who can reach the listener can present a self-signed certificate with an issuer distinguished name matching the public cluster CA subject and gain cluster superuser access, allowing disclosure, modification, or disruption of applications, sandboxes, disks, credentials, and other managed resources. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.1.

items.summary: MISP contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the Galaxy import/sync functionality (captureGalaxy in app/Model/Galaxy.php). The captureGalaxy() method matched an incoming galaxy payload to an existing galaxy by UUID and unconditionally overwrote the matched record, regardless of whether the importing user belonged to the owning organization or whether the galaxy was a system-provided default galaxy. Any authenticated user holding the perm_galaxy_editor role could therefore: (1) demote a default galaxy by setting its default flag to false, (2) reassign the galaxy's org_id and orgc_id to the attacker's organization, effectively taking ownership, and (3) modify other galaxy fields (name, description, distribution, version). Additionally, the role-level permission check (perm_site_admin or perm_galaxy_editor) was executed after the captureOrganisationAndSG() call, meaning organization and sharing-group data was already captured before the authorization decision was made. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the perm_galaxy_editor role and the ability to submit a galaxy import payload containing a UUID that matches an existing galaxy. The security impact is loss of data integrity across the MISP instance: default galaxy definitions are corrupted, cross-organization ownership is silently transferred, and the integrity of shared threat-intelligence galaxy metadata is compromised for all users of the instance.

items.summary:
MISP contains an authorization flaw in the GalaxyCluster model's captureCluster() function, which handles the import and synchronization of Galaxy Clusters. Prior to the fix, any authenticated user holding the galaxy editor role could replace an existing locked Galaxy Cluster by supplying its UUID in an import request, regardless of which organization owned the cluster. The function unconditionally called captureOrganisationAndSG() before the save operation, overwriting the cluster's org_id and orgc_id fields with the importing user's organization, effectively transferring ownership of the cluster to the attacker's organization. Additionally, the save operation was not restricted to a specific set of fields, allowing arbitrary field modification.

The vulnerable behavior required the attacker to possess a valid MISP account with the perm_galaxy_editor role and to know or discover the UUID of a target cluster belonging to another organization. No site-admin or owner-organization privilege was enforced for the update path. The result was that a low-privilege galaxy editor in one organization could modify the content (value, description, distribution, etc.) of clusters owned by other organizations and seize ownership, corrupting the integrity of shared threat-intelligence data across the MISP instance.

The vulnerability was reported by ENISA and CERT.pl. The fix introduces an explicit authorization gate that restricts cluster updates to the owner organization, a sync user who can see the cluster via sharing-group rules, or a site administrator, and enforces a field allow-list that excludes org_id and orgc_id from update writes, preserving original ownership.

items.summary: MISP contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the Sighting model when the Sightings_anonymise setting is enabled. The listSightings and sightings/restSearch endpoints accepted a caller-supplied org_id filter parameter and applied it directly to the SQL query without verifying whether the requesting user was authorized to filter by that organisation. Because the anonymization mechanism masks the reporter's organisation in the returned records, a non-site-admin user could bypass the anonymization by specifying another organisation's ID in the filter. The query would then return only that organisation's sightings, effectively naming the reporter and defeating the purpose of the anonymization feature. A negated filter (NOT IN) similarly revealed which sightings belonged to the target organisation by exclusion. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with sighting read permissions (perm_sighting) who is not a site administrator, and the Sightings_anonymise plugin setting must be enabled. items.summary: MISP contains an access control flaw in its tag management endpoints: events/addTag (single and bulk), events/removeTag, and attributes/removeTag. These endpoints loaded their target event or attribute using an unscoped database query (recursive = -1) that did not apply the calling user's ACL visibility rules. As a result, two distinct security issues existed: (1) Information disclosure: the removeTag endpoint returned different responses depending on whether a given tag was present on a hidden event, allowing an authenticated user to enumerate which tags were applied to events they had no visibility into. (2) Unauthorized modification: users belonging to the host organisation, who are permitted to set local tags on records they can see, could add or remove local tags on events and attributes they could not see, because the canModifyTag ACL check operated on the unscoped object without first verifying the caller's visibility. The fix replaces the unscoped find() calls with ACL-aware fetch methods (fetchSimpleEvent and fetchAttributeSimple) that apply the user's visibility before the object is returned, and adds an explicit empty-object check in removeTag so that a hidden event responds identically to a non-existent one. Affected components include the EventsController (addTag, removeTag), the AttributesController (removeTag), and the ACLComponent (canModifyTag). The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with at least the tagger role (perm_tagger) or host-organisation membership.

items.summary:
MISP contains an authorization bypass in its event search and filter functionality. When a user performed searches through events/restSearch (value, value prefix, searchall, type, uuid, attribute tags, object filters), objects/restSearch, or the event index tag, galaxy, and quick filters, the underlying SQL subqueries matched against attributes and objects without enforcing the per-attribute distribution, sharing-group, or soft-deleted visibility rules that apply when fetching individual elements.

A user who could view an event (for example, a community-distributed event) could therefore use search to determine whether organisation-only, sharing-group-restricted, or soft-deleted attributes and objects existed within that event. Because the value filter supports prefix matching (LIKE), an attacker could enumerate the full value of a hidden attribute one character at a time. Tags attached exclusively to hidden attributes also leaked through the tag, galaxy, and quick-filter paths on the event index.

The vulnerability affects the EventsController quick-filter and index-filter logic, the Event model wildcard/value/uuid/tag filter methods, the MispAttribute tag filter, the MispObject buildFilterConditions and restSearch methods, and the ReportFromEvent object filter. Site administrators and users belonging to the event's own organisation retain full visibility, and sync users continue to match soft-deleted elements as intended.

The issue was reported by ENISA.

items.summary: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the user login-email change logic. When an external authentication backend is configured (LDAP, Shibboleth, ApacheSecureAuth, or CustomAuth), the login email address serves as the key by which the directory service resolves a user's identity, organization, and role on each login. The __canChangeLogin() method in UsersController only checked the MISP.disable_user_login_change setting and site-admin status; it did not account for whether an external authentication backend was active. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user (including org admins) could change their own login email to an address that matches a higher-privilege account in the external directory. On the user's next login, the external backend would resolve that email to the target directory identity, granting the attacker the organization and role associated with that identity. This constitutes an account-identity capture and privilege escalation: the attacker effectively assumes the identity of any directory account whose email they can guess or discover. The vulnerability requires an authenticated session with a valid API key or session token and a MISP instance configured with at least one external authentication backend. The impact is limited to the scope of the captured directory identity's privileges within MISP.

items.summary: libp2p is a JavaScript implementation of the libp2p networking stack. Prior to 17.0.0, the @libp2p/gossipsub default configuration allows a connected remote peer to submit unsigned subscription RPC metadata for arbitrarily many distinct topic strings. handleReceivedSubscription in packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts creates a persistent topics-map entry for each accepted topic, while allowedTopics is unset by default, decodeRpc maxSubscriptions limits only one RPC rather than aggregate topic bytes, and peer scoring has no subscription-volume penalty. A single peer can therefore grow the topics map and committed heap toward out-of-memory conditions, and disconnecting additionally causes removePeer to scan all accumulated topic entries. This issue is fixed in version 17.0.0.

items.summary: libp2p is a JavaScript implementation of the libp2p networking stack. Prior to 5.1.22, the @libp2p/crypto code reached by the default Identify service accepts a remote peer’s crafted publicKey before peer-id or signature verification and passes it through publicKeyFromProtobuf to the ASN.1 DER decoder. readLength in packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts accepts long-form element lengths larger than the remaining buffer, causing readInteger and related readers to loop synchronously over an attacker-claimed length from a very small key blob. Because decoding occurs in one event-loop tick before the remotePeer equality check in packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts, the Identify timeout cannot interrupt it, allowing repeated unauthenticated connections to stall all timers and peers and transiently exhaust memory. This issue is fixed in version 5.1.22.

From 3.0.0 until 3.7.9, 4.1.2, and 5.1.2, the Curator media panel accepts image/svg+xml files by default and stores and serves their markup inline without sanitization. An authenticated user with media-upload permission can store an SVG containing scripts, event-handler attributes, or javascript: URIs. When another panel user selects the View action, the SVG opens as a top-level browser document and its active content executes in the Filament application's origin. The script can perform authenticated same-origin actions as the viewing user and read same-origin data and script-accessible tokens. Panel thumbnails are not affected because they render through an image element that does not execute SVG script. This issue is fixed in versions 3.7.9, 4.1.2, and 5.1.2.

items.summary: qbee-agent is the device agent component of the qbee.io IoT device management platform. Prior to 2026.27, the privileged createFile helper followed attacker-controlled symbolic links during file creation. A local unprivileged user whose account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle could replace ~/.ssh with a link to /root/.ssh, causing the agent to write an authorized key for root. On systems using RAUC download mode with ineffective kernel symlink protection, the predictable /tmp/.bundle.raucb.part path could be linked to a system file and then overwritten or truncated during an update. A file-distribution destination beneath an attacker-controlled directory could similarly redirect the partial-download path so the agent changed ownership of a sensitive file. These vectors could result in root privilege escalation, arbitrary file modification, or denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 2026.27.

items.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.0, failed Railpack builds and database backups propagate an execution error containing the full command, exposing application environment variables, database passwords, and S3 access keys embedded in those commands. items.summary:
tcp_pkt_linearize() in subsys/net/ip/tcp.c is used by th_get() whenever a received TCP header is not contiguous in a single net_buf. While pulling the header bytes out of the following fragments, the loop called net_buf_unref() on an emptied fragment without first detaching its frags pointer. net_buf_unref() walks the whole fragment list, so the payload buffers still linked behind that fragment were freed as well, and the stale pointer was then reinstalled into the packet as buf->frags, producing a use-after-free and a later double free during packet teardown. The same loop also advanced to second->frags unconditionally: when the fragment still held payload after the header remainder was pulled, it was spliced out of the packet without ever being unreferenced, permanently leaking that buffer and silently dropping the data it carried.

The defect is reached from tcp_recv() via th_get() on every received TCP segment, before connection lookup or any header validation, so a single unauthenticated segment that matches a listening socket is sufficient. An attacker only needs the TCP header to straddle a net_buf boundary, which they can arrange from off-link: IPv6 extension headers are accepted on receive and their length is added to the header offset by th_get(), so a Destination Options header of a suitable length places the TCP header across the boundary of the fixed-size receive buffers (CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE). Packet chains assembled from several sources - IPv4/IPv6 reassembly, 6LoWPAN/802.15.4 reassembly, tunnel or virtual interfaces that strip an outer header, or drivers producing scatter-gather chains - can additionally present a short interior fragment that the loop empties exactly, which is the case that frees the remainder of the packet while it is still in use.

The reliably reachable consequence is exhaustion of the receive buffer pool: each crafted segment leaks one net_buf from the fixed CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT pool, the buffers are never reclaimed, and once the pool is empty the device can no longer receive network traffic until it is rebooted. Where a fragment is emptied exactly, the impact rises to memory corruption: freed pool buffers are written through by the remainder of the loop, their contents may be delivered to the application, and the packet is double-freed on teardown.

The fix saves and clears second->frags before the net_buf_unref() so only the emptied header fragment is released, and advances to the next fragment only when second->len == 0, keeping any fragment that still holds payload in the packet. This restores the detach-before-unref ownership pattern used elsewhere in the stack, for example in net_pkt_trim_buffer().

The mail parser does not reject Apache .htaccess configuration files or PHP-executable files when saving ticket attachments. The issue was fixed in commit d5059b1.

items.summary:
LMS (Lan Management System) is vulnerable to privilege escalation in the lmsd daemon. The daemon loads the libraries listed in the LMS database without checking that they come from a trusted location. An attacker with access to the web server process or with write access to the LMS database can register a malicious library and trigger a configuration reload, causing lmsd to load and execute it. Because the example systemd unit does not set a separate user, lmsd runs as root, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges.
This issue was fixed in commit 89dd3f7. The lmsd component was removed. For existing installations that use lmsd, the recommended solution is to disable and remove this component.

The unrecovered panic can terminate the request goroutine or the service process. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.0.

items.summary: FreeSWITCH is a Software Defined Telecom Stack enabling the digital transformation from proprietary telecom switches to a software implementation that runs on any commodity hardware. Prior to 1.11.2, after FreeSWITCH has learned and closed source learning for an RTP peer, read_rtp_packet() and rtp_common_read() in src/switch_rtp.c reject RTP from an unrecognized source only after packet classification and, for encrypted calls, SRTP processing. An unauthenticated attacker with UDP reachability to an active RTP or SRTP media port can sustain a foreign-source packet flood that occupies the media read path and prevents legitimate media from entering FreeSWITCH on calls that consume incoming media for relay or echo. The resulting one-way audio allows the affected endpoint to continue hearing the other party, but the other party loses that endpoint's audio, leaving SIP signaling established while the call is unusable for conversation. Transmit-only playback was unaffected in testing. A caller can learn the media port from the SDP answer, while a third party must first discover an active port, and no valid SRTP key is required. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.2.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

PCI: altera: Fix resource leaks on probe failure

The chained IRQ handler is set during probe, but is only removed during the
driver remove(). If pci_host_probe() fails, the handler and INTx IRQ
domain remain set even though the devm-managed host bridge storage
containing struct altera_pcie will be released, leaving the handler with
a stale data pointer.

Interrupts are also enabled before pci_host_probe() is called. If probe
fails after that point, the controller interrupt source should be disabled
before the chained handler and INTx domain are removed.

So set the chained handler only after the INTx domain has been created.
Disable controller interrupts during IRQ teardown, and tear the IRQ setup
down if pci_host_probe() fails.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: firewire: isight: bound the sample count to the packet payload

isight_packet() takes the frame count from the device iso packet and
checks it only against the device claimed iso length.

	count = be32_to_cpu(payload->sample_count);
	if (likely(count <= (length - 16) / 4))
		isight_samples(isight, payload->samples, count);

length is the iso header data_length. It can be up to 0xffff. So the
gate allows a count up to about 16379. isight_samples() then copies
count frames out of payload->samples into the PCM DMA buffer.

payload->samples holds only 2 * MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET values. The
device multiplexes two samples per frame. A count past
MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET reads past the payload. A count past the buffer
size writes past runtime->dma_area. The smallest PCM buffer is larger
than MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET. Bounding the count to MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET
keeps both the read and the write in range.

A malicious or faulty Apple iSight on the FireWire bus reaches this
during a normal capture.

Add the MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET bound to the gate.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: usx2y: us144mkii: fix work UAF on disconnect

tascam_disconnect() cancels capture_work and midi_in_work before
usb_kill_anchored_urbs() kills the capture/MIDI-in URBs.  Those URBs
self-resubmit, and their completion handlers reschedule the work.

A URB that completes in the small window between cancel_work_sync() and
usb_kill_anchored_urbs() therefore re-arms the work after its only
cancel.  Nothing cancels it again before snd_card_free() frees the
card-private tascam structure, so the work handler then runs on freed
memory.

Kill the anchored URBs before cancelling the work; once the work is
cancelled no remaining URB can complete to re-arm it.

iio: temperature: tmp006: use devm_iio_trigger_register

tmp006_probe() allocates the DRDY trigger with devm_iio_trigger_alloc()
but registers it with plain iio_trigger_register(). The driver has no
.remove() callback, so on module unload the trigger stays in the global
trigger list while its memory is freed by devm, leaving a dangling
entry.

Switch to devm_iio_trigger_register() so the registration is undone in
the same devm scope as the allocation.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

erofs: disable LZ4 rolling decompression for now

LZ4 rolling decompression [1] was introduced to reduce the memory
footprint of temporary pages:

 For many cases, it is needed for users to read small data within
 a compressed extent (pcluster), either due to random small read, or
 since uptodate folios (typically order-0) cannot be reused for
 decompression again since decompression algorithm refills
 already-uptodate folios.

Rolling decompression works because LZ4 is LZ77-based and only refers
to the most recent 64 KiB of decompressed data, so in theory only a
bounded rolling window of temporary pages is needed when decompressing.

It can save a lot of temporary memory, e.g.
 601,960-byte data can be compressed into a 256k LZ4 compressed extent,
 which means it needs 146 extra pages per request in the worst case if
 rolling decompression is disabled.

However, the upstream LZ4 implementation is not under EROFS' control:
For example, the literal copy memmove() may still **copy long literals
backward** on x86 based on the address comparison even when the source
and destination ranges do not overlap (IOWs, inline decompression
doesn't need to be considered here). That breaks the rolling assumption
and makes the optimization broken.

Disable it for now to make sure the data correctness first since EROFS
is used everywhere now: The rolling window approach can be revived once
we either ensure that the official LZ4 code always copies forward for
non-overlapping ranges or maintain our own LZ4 implementation in EROFS.

The main impact is a higher runtime memory footprint; However, recent
commit 0f6273ab4637 ("erofs: add a reserved buffer pool for lz4
decompression") helps mitigate this when enabled but it's still not
perfect.

[1] https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc19/presentation/gao
    § 3.3 Decompression

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme: remove stale namespaces by NSID range during scan

nvme_scan_ns_list() drops the stale namespaces in each gap in the
reported NSID list one NSID at a time. Every iteration calls
nvme_find_get_ns() to look the namespace up and removes it if it is
present. The loop runs once per NSID in the gap rather than once per
namespace actually present.

NSIDs are 32-bit, so a target with a sparse NSID space can make a
single gap spin the loop billions of times with nothing to remove.

  watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#4 stuck for 26s!
  Workqueue: nvme-wq nvme_scan_work [nvme_core]
  RIP: 0010:__srcu_read_unlock+0xb/0x20
  Call Trace:
   nvme_find_get_ns+0x7d/0xb0 [nvme_core]
   nvme_scan_ns_list+0xe8/0x280 [nvme_core]
   nvme_scan_work+0x18a/0x280 [nvme_core]
   process_one_work+0x197/0x380
   worker_thread+0x2fe/0x410
   kthread+0xe0/0x100

Rename nvme_remove_invalid_namespaces() to nvme_remove_nsid_range()
and give it an open (start, end) NSID range. ctrl->namespaces is
sorted by NSID, so the whole gap is dropped in a single walk that
stops once end is reached. This bounds the work by the namespaces
that are present instead of by the size of the gap.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iio: adc: ti-ads1119: fix PM reference leak in buffer preenable

ads1119_triggered_buffer_preenable() resumes the device with
pm_runtime_resume_and_get() before starting a conversion.

If i2c_smbus_write_byte() fails, the function returns the error directly
and leaves the runtime PM usage counter elevated. The matching
postdisable callback is not called when preenable fails, so the reference
is leaked and the device may remain runtime-active indefinitely.

Store the I2C transfer result in ret and drop the runtime PM reference on
failure before returning the error.

iio: buffer: hw-consumer: free scan_mask on buffer release

Before that change, the scan mask storage was embedded in struct

That commit moved the scan mask to a separate bitmap_zalloc() allocation
stored in buffer.scan_mask, but left iio_hw_buf_release() unchanged.

Free the scan mask in iio_hw_buf_release() before freeing the buffer
wrapper.

sign gets initialized later.

In addition (and due to the nature of the cleanup), fix a sign-extension
bug where, float32 would get bitwise anded with ~BIT(31)
(which is 0xFFFFFFFF7FFFFFFF) which corrupted the exponent.

bmg160_get_filter() walks bmg160_samp_freq_table[] looking for the entry
matching the bw_bits value read from the chip:

	for (i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE(bmg160_samp_freq_table); ++i) {
		if (bmg160_samp_freq_table[i].bw_bits == bw_bits)
			break;
	}
	*val = bmg160_samp_freq_table[i].filter;

If no entry matches, i ends up equal to the array size and the next line
reads one slot past the end. bmg160_set_filter() has the same shape, driven
by 'val' instead of bw_bits.

smatch flags both:

  drivers/iio/gyro/bmg160_core.c:204 bmg160_get_filter() error:
  buffer overflow 'bmg160_samp_freq_table' 7 <= 7
  drivers/iio/gyro/bmg160_core.c:222 bmg160_set_filter() error:
  buffer overflow 'bmg160_samp_freq_table' 7 <= 7

Return -EINVAL when no entry matches.

The set_filter() path is reachable from userspace via the sysfs
in_anglvel_filter_low_pass_3db_frequency interface, so userspace can
trivially trigger the out-of-bounds read with a value that is not in
bmg160_samp_freq_table[].filter.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/rds: clear cp_flags bits individually in rds_conn_path_reset()

rds_conn_path_reset() wipes the whole flag word with a plain
cp->cp_flags = 0 store.  Every other accessor of that word uses
atomic bitops, and some of them can run concurrently with the reset:
RDS_LL_SEND_FULL is set from rds_send_xmit() and cleared from the
transport completion paths, neither of which holds anything that
excludes the shutdown worker.  A plain store racing an atomic
read-modify-write on the same word is a data race, and whichever
side loses has its update silently discarded.

Clear the two bits the reset is actually responsible for instead.
RDS_IN_XMIT and RDS_RECV_REFILL need no store at all here: they
belong to the caller, rds_conn_shutdown(), which waits for both to be
clear before calling the transport shutdown and this reset.

This also gives every bit in cp_flags a single well-defined writer
discipline, which the following patches rely on when they turn
RDS_IN_XMIT and RDS_RECV_REFILL into bit locks held across the
teardown: a blanket store mid-teardown would destroy lock ownership
that an atomic clear preserves.

Oracle UEK carries the same conversion ("net/rds: Preserve essential
connection state flags"), motivated by its asynchronous shutdown
state machine, whose progress and destroy flags must survive the
reset.  UEK's variant also clears RDS_IN_XMIT and RDS_RECV_REFILL
because there the reset runs as the final step of a teardown that
owns both bits, making those clears its unlock.  Upstream that
release belongs in rds_conn_shutdown(): once a later patch in this
series turns the two bits into locks held across the teardown, ending
ownership needs release semantics and a wake-up that a plain clear
inside the reset would not provide.

Based on Oracle UEK commit "net/rds: Preserve essential connection
state flags" by Gerd Rausch.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/rds: acquire RDS_IN_XMIT in rds_tcp_reset_callbacks()

rds_tcp_reset_callbacks() quiesces the transmit path by setting the
path state to RDS_CONN_RESETTING and then waiting for RDS_IN_XMIT to
be sampled clear before swapping the underlying socket and calling
rds_send_path_reset().

Sampling the bit clear is not the same as owning it: rds_send_xmit()
can re-acquire RDS_IN_XMIT right after the wait_event() returns.  Its
state recheck after taking the lock is a store-buffering pattern (the
resetter writes the state and reads the bit, the sender writes the
bit and reads the state) and acquire_in_xmit() is only an acquire
operation, so on weakly ordered architectures both sides can miss
each other's write and the transmit path then runs concurrently with
rds_send_path_reset() rewriting cp_xmit_* state - which is exactly
what the comment above rds_send_path_reset() tells its callers to
prevent.

Take the lock instead, hold it across the socket swap and
rds_send_path_reset(), and release it with a wake-up at the end.  The
lock-ordering constraint documented above the wait still holds: the
lock is acquired before lock_sock(), so a sender inside tcp_sendmsg()
can never be waited on while we hold the socket lock.

Two details of the old code go away with the same change:

 - t_sock is now read only after the lock is acquired.  The old code
   cached it before waiting; the teardown in rds_conn_shutdown()
   releases that socket and clears t_sock, so a pointer cached before
   the wait can be stale by the time the accept path resumes.  Reading
   it under RDS_IN_XMIT is what makes the exclusion complete once the
   teardown owns the same lock, which the next patch arranges; until
   then the teardown still only samples the bit, and the two paths
   remain as exposed to each other as they are today.

 - The old !osock early path called rds_send_path_reset() with no
   serialization at all.  It now runs under the lock like the normal
   path.  The conditional RDS_CONN_RESETTING transition of the
   previous patch happens before the socket check either way: a path
   found without a socket is either still connecting (its reconnect
   worker blocked on t_conn_path_lock) and legitimately goes
   RESETTING -> UP on the new socket, or it has been torn down
   meanwhile and is dropped.

The in-function comment describing the old wait-based quiesce is
rewritten to describe the lock-based one, and the stale block comment
above the function (which still described a return value and an
incomplete list of t_sock writers) is refreshed to name all four
writers - the connect, accept, teardown and swap paths - and what
serializes each of them.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/rds: acquire the fastpath locks in rds_conn_shutdown()

rds_conn_shutdown() quiesces the transmit and receive-refill paths by
waiting for RDS_IN_XMIT and RDS_RECV_REFILL to be sampled clear, and
then runs the transport shutdown and rds_conn_path_reset().  Sampling
the bits clear is not the same as owning them: the moment after the
wait_event() returns, rds_send_xmit() can re-acquire RDS_IN_XMIT (or
rds_ib_recv_refill() can re-acquire RDS_RECV_REFILL) and run
concurrently with the teardown.

The sender does recheck the connection state after taking the lock,
but that recheck is a classic store-buffering pattern: teardown writes
the state and reads the bit while the sender writes the bit and reads
the state.  acquire_in_xmit() is only an acquire operation, so on
weakly ordered architectures both sides can miss each other's write,
and the transmit path then runs while the transport zeroes its rings
(e.g. rds_ib_ring_init()) and rds_send_path_reset() rewrites the
transmit state under it.

by making the teardown path *acquire* the fastpath bit locks instead
of testing them ("rds: Make sure transmit path and connection
tear-down does not run concurrently").  Ownership of a single word is
decided by RMW atomicity, so no cross-variable ordering is needed.

Do the same here: take both locks before calling the transport
shutdown, hold them across rds_conn_path_reset(), and release them
explicitly with a wake-up afterwards.  Both are released with
clear_bit_unlock(), so that the ring re-initialization done by the
transport shutdown and the transmit state rewritten by
rds_send_path_reset() are ordered before either bit is seen clear by
the next acquire_in_xmit() or acquire_refill().

The fastpath users of these bits - rds_send_xmit() and
rds_ib_recv_refill() - are trylock style and back off while teardown
owns the locks, so no new lock dependency is introduced for them.

spans the teardown instead of at most one send batch.  That waiter

and holds rds_tcp_accept_lock and t_conn_path_lock while it waits, so
a duelling SYN accepted while its path is being torn down parks
accept processing for the duration of the teardown - for TCP bounded
by the (up to 5 s) drain loop in rds_tcp_conn_path_shutdown().  An IB

blocking waiter either: rds_tcp_reset_callbacks() is the only blocking
acquirer of these bits and waits only on its own TCP path, and the
fastpaths are trylock-and-back-off on both transports, so a long IB
drain lengthens only that path's own quiesce.  The
window is narrow: the accept-side state check has to pass before the
teardown moves the path to RDS_CONN_DISCONNECTING.

Because krdsd is a single global workqueue, everything else queued

during namespace teardown - waits behind the parked accept worker for
that time.  It cannot deadlock, although the waits do point at each

Prior to 16.1.1, the anonymous Push Notification SNS callback handled by SnsMessageResource falls back to a CTS predicate blob after a messageId expires from the in-memory dispatcher, treats top-level blob keys as Java class names for Class.forName, and deserializes attacker-controlled JSON through Jackson. A low-privileged user who starts Push Registration and obtains the messageId, shared secret, and challenge can wait for expiry, replace the persistent blob through anonymous callbacks, and trigger class loading and construction in the OpenAM JVM. The primitive can cause classpath-dependent process execution, file writes, or denial of service, although command execution was not confirmed on the tested stock classpath. This issue is fixed in version 16.1.1.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iio: adc: lpc32xx: Initialize completion before requesting IRQ

In the report from Jaeyoung Chung:

"lpc32xx_adc_probe() in drivers/iio/adc/lpc32xx_adc.c registers its
interrupt handler with devm_request_irq() before it initializes
st->completion with init_completion(). If an interrupt arrives after
devm_request_irq() and before init_completion(), the handler calls
complete() on an uninitialized completion, causing a kernel panic.

The probe path, in lpc32xx_adc_probe():

    iodev = devm_iio_device_alloc(&pdev->dev, sizeof(*st)); /* st kzalloc-zeroed */
    ...
    retval = devm_request_irq(&pdev->dev, irq, lpc32xx_adc_isr, 0,
                              LPC32XXAD_NAME, st);           /* register handler */
    ...
    init_completion(&st->completion);                       /* initialize completion */

lpc32xx_adc_isr() calls complete():

    complete(&st->completion);

If the device raises an interrupt before init_completion() runs,
complete() acquires the uninitialized wait.lock and walks the zeroed
task_list in swake_up_locked(). The zeroed task_list makes list_empty()
return false, so swake_up_locked() dereferences a NULL list entry,
triggering a KASAN wild-memory-access."

Fix the chance of a spurious IRQ causing an uninitialized pointer
dereference by moving init_completion() above devm_request_irq().
